Note · Cusumano, Gawer & Yoffie — The Business of Platforms

4 min read814 wordsUpdated 2026-06-06notes/canon/canon-cusumano-business-of-platforms.md

Canon · Cluster: Network Effects & Platform Strategy · Maps to Course 04 (Competitive Strategy), E10 (Digital & AI Transformation)

  • Source: Michael Cusumano, Annabelle Gawer & David Yoffie, The Business of Platforms (2019)
  • Core claim: Not all platforms are alike — and the durable ones manage a few brutal strategic tensions deliberately.
  • Framework:
  • Two types: Innovation platforms (others build on top of you — iOS, AWS, Salesforce) vs. transaction platforms (you facilitate exchange — Uber, Airbnb, marketplaces). The most durable are hybrids.
  • The hard strategic choices:
    • How open? — too open loses control/quality; too closed limits growth.
    • How to price each side? — usually subsidize the harder-to-attract side (canon hagiu wright multi sided platforms).
    • Multi-homing — users on multiple platforms weaken your network effects; raise switching costs or exclusivity to fight it.
    • Platform envelopment — when (and whether) to compete with your own ecosystem partners; it always creates tension and can poison the ecosystem.
  • Applies when: running or investing in a platform that must decide openness, pricing, and how to treat its own complementors.
  • Breaks when: the strategic-choice menu is clean but executing it is political and dynamic — the "compete with your ecosystem?" call (Sherlocking) buys short-term revenue at long-term trust cost, and the book can't tell you the threshold. Also written near the techlash/antitrust inflection — the "envelop everything" playbook now collides with regulation in ways the framework underweights. Complementor relationships are the unstable co-opetition of canon brandenburger nalebuff coopetition at scale.
  • Practitioner counterpoint: (researched 2026-06-05 — Talks at Google / NFX transcript corpus; r/startups thin) Operators reframe Cusumano's "manage the tensions" as a sequencing problem: you can't envelop, price, or fight multi-homing on a network that doesn't exist yet. Andrew Chen (The Cold Start Problem, Talks at Google) insists the early network is hand-built, not designed — the founders who won "sat down, and they did the work… they manually did it, and then they found ways to operationalize it." NFX sharpens the why it's worth it: of four defensibilities (scale, switching costs, brand, network effects), the network effect is "the greatest of them all… because it's native to the digital environment" — "the more users you get… the more ahead you'll get of your competitors, so the faster you go the faster you go." The practitioner caution the book underplays: viral growth is not a network effect ("a viral effect is about acquisition… they're actually very different things") — cheap acquisition can mask a network that never reaches the tipping point.
  • Researched layer (2026-06-05)
  • Canonical explanation (sourced): the engine under both platform types is demand-side economies of scale — "more users leads to more value for existing users… so we call this strong demand-side economies of scale" (David Halliday, "2-Sided Markets"). Where a traditional firm profits on a markup over cost of goods, a transaction platform "never has a traditional cost of goods sold… [it] exists to facilitate that transaction," and at scale these markets tip toward "winner-take-all… markets where barriers to entry grow dramatically as the incumbent companies are growing." That tipping dynamic is exactly why Cusumano's openness/pricing/multi-homing choices are existential rather than cosmetic.
  • Real application (mined): the Airbnb cold-start, told from the demand side — early on "no pictures, no inventory, no booking. You literally would just email them" (Andrew Chen). The fix was a hand-built atomic network ("the smallest network that can stand on its own"), repeated until "the tipping point, which is when you're able to create these networks on demand… and then escape velocity." The Halliday transcript names the flip side: as 2011–12 Airbnb filled up, "that raises price and… decreases the overall availability" — early subsidy and abundance erode once the market clears, the practical face of Cusumano's "how to price each side."
  • Where the corpus pushes back on the book: the transcripts argue the binding constraint isn't choosing among strategic tensions — it's reaching critical mass at all. Defensibility is earned by manual, un-scalable early work and by not mistaking viral acquisition for a genuine network effect (NFX). Cusumano's clean two-type taxonomy says little about the messy, operations-heavy zero-to-tipping-point phase where most platforms actually die.
